extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, communications students, and PR strategists
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-style guidance laying out ethical standards and practical principles for public relations work, including media framing, crisis response, technology use, cultural competence, and ongoing professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press frames and interprets information
rubrics_metrics.description: The press doesn’t merely convey information; it interprets and frames it, affecting how the public perceives that information. Headlines, images, and the tone of an article can significantly color the audience's reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how headlines, images and tone will shape perception and plan messages accordingly. Understand that media selection and presentation are part of the communication outcome; work to influence framing without manipulating facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with media to ensure accurate, effective conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must work collaboratively with media outlets, employing strategic techniques to ensure their messages are accurately and effectively conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop relationships with journalists, provide clear materials, and use strategic timing and messaging to harness the power of the press to inform and persuade. Treat media engagement as a cooperative process to maximize accurate transmission of key points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to a strict code of honesty and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are compelled to adhere to a strict code of honesty and transparency; while the goal may be to cast the organization in a favorable light, this should never be at the expense of truthfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deception or deliberate omission. Any attempt to mislead jeopardizes foundational trust and can have severe consequences for both organization and practitioner. Make transparency a baseline practice in materials and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of disseminated information is non-negotiable
rubrics_metrics.description: The integrity of the information disseminated is, therefore, a non‑negotiable principle in the ethical practice of public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts, cite sources where appropriate, correct errors promptly, and ensure that communications do not distort or omit material information. Treat accuracy as ethical duty, not just PR effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance organizational objectives with the public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations professionals must navigate the delicate balance between organizational objectives and the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh short-term organizational gains against long-term public trust. Plan communications that advance objectives while respecting the public’s right to full and honest information; consider stakeholder consequences when forming strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge potential risks and side effects
rubrics_metrics.description: While a company may wish to highlight the benefits of a new product, it is equally important to acknowledge any potential risks or side effects associated with its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose material risks in messaging so the public can make informed decisions. Failure to acknowledge risks undermines informed consent and can erode trust; incorporate balanced benefit/risk framing where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize public safety over immediate financial loss (crisis ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: In crisis situations, prioritize public safety over immediate financial loss — exemplified by Johnson & Johnson’s nationwide Tylenol recall and introduction of tamper‑evident packaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public safety is implicated, take decisive, transparent actions even if costly. Use case studies (e.g., Tylenol recall) to justify recall/withdrawal decisions and to demonstrate long‑term trust restoration strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unethical practices and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unethical practices in public relations can lead to disastrous outcomes (for example, reputational fallout from the BP oil spill); as PR becomes more sophisticated, the potential for manipulation increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be vigilant against tactics that manipulate or deceive. Establish internal ethical checks, review campaigns for potential harm or misleading elements, and favor strategies that build lasting trust rather than short‑term spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure strategies do not deceive or mislead; foster informed communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must ensure that their strategies do not deceive or mislead the public but instead foster informed and engaged communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications to educate and engage rather than obscure. Use clear language, make corrective statements when needed, and provide channels for public feedback and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate technology, social media and data analytics
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital platforms, social media, and big data analytics are integral to modern PR strategy; these tools expand reach and allow for real‑time engagement and feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop proficiency in digital literacy and data interpretation. Use analytics to measure sentiment/effectiveness and to inform iterative improvements, while applying ethical constraints to data use (privacy, consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize transparency and authenticity in messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: There will be an increased emphasis on transparency and authenticity; in an age of accessible information and public skepticism, maintaining trust is paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authentic voice, disclose motives and relationships when relevant, and align messages with demonstrated organizational behavior. Authenticity should be operationalized (policies, spokesperson training) not just claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop cultural competence for globalized communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Globalization presents opportunities and challenges: practitioners will need to be culturally competent, understanding and respecting diverse values and norms across regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt messaging to local norms without compromising core ethical standards. Use local research and consultation to craft communications that resonate while avoiding cultural insensitivity or one‑size‑fits‑all approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit to lifelong learning and professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued education and ethical vigilance are critical; practitioners should seek ongoing professional development to stay abreast of trends, technologies, and ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in courses, certifications, workshops, and professional organizations to maintain competence. Institutionalize learning practices (post‑campaign reviews, ethics training) to adapt to changing media landscapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PR as strategic management of reputation, brand and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations has evolved from publicity to a sophisticated practice crucial for crafting and maintaining reputation, brand identity, and public engagement for individuals, organizations, and nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat PR as a long‑term strategic function tied to organizational goals. Integrate reputation management, brand strategy, and stakeholder engagement into planning and evaluation metrics rather than treating communications as ad‑hoc publicity.
